title: Greedy Best-First vs Hills of Valparaíso!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race across Valparaíso’s steep street layout, choosing the next step by the closest-to-goal estimate. The visualization highlights how fast heuristics find routes, and where they can get trapped on real-world geometry.
ig_caption:
🗺️⛰️ **Valparaíso streets, meet Greedy Best-First**

In this reel, Greedy Best-First builds a path on a graph of real streets: **nodes = intersections** and **edges = road segments**. The algorithm always expands the frontier node with the **lowest heuristic h(n)** (estimated distance to the goal), guided by a priority queue—⚡ fast decisions, no guarantees of optimality.

📌 **Deep technical idea:** it’s a best-first graph search that behaves like:
- **f(n) = h(n)** (ignoring accumulated cost g(n))
- Great when the heuristic is well-aligned with the true shortest path
- Can overshoot into “looks-close” dead-ends when geography (like hills) bends distances

🌐 We used **real-map-like connectivity** (street graphs) to mirror how routing heuristics work in practice—this is why heuristic choice matters in graph theory.

👉 Want a version with A* (adds g(n)) to compare behavior on the same map? Comment **“A*”** and hit ❤️ for more pathfinding visuals!

fb_caption:
🚦 Pathfinding on a real street-style graph!

This visualization uses **Greedy Best-First**: at each step it picks the next intersection that appears closest to the destination using a heuristic estimate. It’s a classic graph search strategy (nodes/edges + priority queue) that’s often quick, but can miss the shortest path—perfect for comparing heuristics on real-world street connectivity.
